title: Physical layout
summary: Placing thousands of cells by simulated annealing so the wires stay short.

ideas.how: placement moves ready-made cells, not single transistors

challenges.title: Watch annealing work
challenges.task: Change the cooling schedule and see wire length fall.

learn.plain: Placement is like arranging seats at a huge dinner so people who talk the most sit closest. Shorter wires mean faster signals and less wasted power.
learn.engineer: Production placers use analytical global placement (smoothed wirelength models such as log-sum-exp or weighted-average plus a density penalty, as in ePlace and RePlAce), then legalization and detailed placement, with timing- and congestion-driven weights. Buffering and clock-tree synthesis follow. Backside power delivery on TSMC A16 and Intel 18A frees front-side routing tracks and changes how standard cells are designed.

options: A list of cells and the wires that connect them
quiz.why: Synthesis produces the netlist; placement and routing turn it into a physical layout.

quiz.q: What does placement try to minimize?
quiz.why: Short wires are faster and use less power; avoiding congestion keeps the design routable.

quiz.q: Why does simulated annealing sometimes accept a worse swap?
options: To escape local traps while the temperature is high
quiz.why: Accepting some bad moves early lets the search find a much better overall layout.

ask: How do tools place billions of cells?
